title: Aviva Travel Insurance Review
meta_title: Aviva Travel Insurance Review 2026: Don't Buy the Basic Tier
meta_description: Aviva's Basic tier pays £1,000 cancellation and £500 baggage. Gold pays £5,000 and £2,500. The tier gap matters more than the price.
intro:
Aviva sells travel insurance across four tiers — Basic, Silver, Gold and Lifetime — and the difference between them is far larger than most comparison tables make clear. Cancellation cover runs from £1,000 on Basic to £5,000 on Gold. Baggage runs from £500 to £2,500.

Those Basic figures are the ones to watch. A £1,000 cancellation limit will not cover a family package holiday, and £500 of baggage cover is roughly one suitcase. Aviva's own documentation describes Basic as the legal-minimum tier and advises against it for travel outside Europe.

If you buy Aviva on price alone and land on Basic, you have bought something quite different from what most people mean by travel insurance.

key_facts.label: Annual multi-trip
key_facts.value: 31 days per trip as standard, extendable to 60 or 90 days for extra premium

key_facts.label: Upper age limit
key_facts.value: None on single trip; annual multi-trip capped at 79 for new policies

key_facts.label: Pre-existing conditions
key_facts.value: Covered after online medical screening; most accepted with a premium loading

sections.heading: The tier gap in real numbers
sections.html:
Take a family of four on a £3,500 package holiday who have to cancel a fortnight before departure.

  • Basic caps cancellation at £1,000. You are roughly £2,500 out of pocket.
  • Silver caps at £3,000. You are £500 short.
  • Gold caps at £5,000. You are covered.

The premium difference between these tiers is usually a fraction of that shortfall. This is the single most common way people discover their travel insurance was inadequate, and it happens at the claim rather than at purchase.

The practical rule: your cancellation limit must exceed the total non-refundable cost of your trip. Add up flights, accommodation and any pre-booked excursions before choosing a tier, rather than picking the cheapest and hoping.

sections.heading: No excess buy-down, which is genuinely unusual
sections.html:
Most UK travel insurers let you pay a little more to reduce or remove the excess. Aviva does not.

That leaves you with £150 per claim on Basic, £100 on Silver and £75 on Gold and Lifetime, with no way to buy it down. Note the excess is charged per claim, not per policy — so a trip where your luggage goes missing and you also need medical treatment can generate two separate excesses.

For small claims this matters more than the headline limits. A £220 replacement phone on a Basic policy nets you £70 after excess, which is rarely worth the paperwork. If you expect to make small claims, the Gold excess of £75 changes that arithmetic significantly.

sections.heading: Where Aviva is genuinely strong
sections.html:
Medical cover is not the weak point at any tier. Even Basic carries £5 million, and Gold carries £15 million. Serious medical repatriation is the scenario that bankrupts uninsured travellers, and Aviva covers it properly throughout the range.

No upper age limit on single-trip policies. That is a real differentiator. Many mainstream insurers cut off at 75 or 80, pushing older travellers towards specialist providers at higher prices. Aviva will write a single-trip policy at any age.

Pre-existing conditions are handled sensibly. Online medical screening, most conditions accepted with a premium loading rather than a flat refusal. Complex cardiac, oncology or respiratory histories may need additional underwriting, but the default posture is to quote rather than decline.

120 days on a single trip is longer than many competitors allow, which suits extended travel or a long winter stay abroad.

sections.heading: The annual multi-trip catch
sections.html:
Annual policies cap each individual trip at 31 days as standard. You can extend to 60 or 90 days by paying more, but the default catches people who assume an annual policy means unlimited duration.

The second catch is the age 79 cut-off for new annual policies, which sits oddly beside the unlimited age on single trip. If you are approaching 80 and travel several times a year, you will end up buying single-trip cover repeatedly — usually more expensive in total than an annual policy would have been.

Worth doing the arithmetic before assuming annual is cheaper: for two or three short European trips a year, single-trip policies at Gold level often cost less than an annual policy at Silver.

pros: Medical cover is strong at every tier, from £5m on Basic to £15m on Gold
No upper age limit on single-trip policies, unlike many mainstream insurers
Pre-existing conditions accepted after screening, usually with a loading rather than a refusal
Single trips up to 120 days, longer than many competitors permit
Gold excess of £75 is competitive for a mainstream insurer
cons: Basic tier caps cancellation at £1,000 and baggage at £500 — inadequate for most package holidays
No excess buy-down option, which most UK insurers offer
Excess applies per claim, so one trip can generate several
Annual multi-trip limits each trip to 31 days unless you pay to extend
Annual policies unavailable to new customers over 79
Aviva's own documents advise against Basic outside Europe, which raises the question of why it is sold
verdict: A solid choice at Gold or Lifetime, and a poor one at Basic. Add up your total non-refundable trip cost first and pick the tier whose cancellation limit exceeds it — that single decision matters more than which insurer you choose. Aviva is particularly worth considering if you are over 75 and travelling on a single trip, since the absence of an upper age limit is rare among mainstream insurers. Look elsewhere if you want to buy the excess down, or if you need annual cover and are approaching 80.

faqs.q: Which Aviva tier should I buy?
faqs.a: Whichever one has a cancellation limit above the total non-refundable cost of your trip. Basic covers £1,000, Silver £3,000, Gold and Lifetime £5,000. For a package holiday costing more than £1,000, Basic will leave you short.

faqs.q: Does Aviva cover pre-existing medical conditions?
faqs.a: Yes, following online medical screening. Most conditions are accepted with a premium loading. Complex cardiac, oncology or respiratory cases may need additional underwriting.

faqs.q: Is there an upper age limit?
faqs.a: Not on single-trip policies. Annual multi-trip policies are capped at age 79 for new customers.
No. Aviva does not offer an excess buy-down, which is unusual among UK travel insurers. You pay £150 on Basic, £100 on Silver or £75 on Gold and Lifetime, per claim.

faqs.q: How long can a single trip be?
faqs.a: Up to 120 consecutive days. Annual multi-trip policies allow 31 days per trip as standard, extendable to 60 or 90 days for an additional premium.

title: Saga Travel Insurance Review
meta_title: Saga Travel Insurance Review 2026: £20m Medical, No Age Cap
meta_description: Saga covers over-50s only, with £20m medical, £20,000 cancellation and no upper age limit. Cruise cover is included as standard.
intro:
Saga writes travel insurance for people aged 50 and over, and nobody else. That restriction is the whole point of the product: rather than treating older travellers as an awkward edge case to be surcharged, the entire policy is built around them.

It shows in the limits. The Plus tier carries £20 million of emergency medical cover and £20,000 for cancellation — four times Aviva's top-tier cancellation limit. There is no upper age limit at all, and cruise cover is included as standard rather than sold as an add-on.

The trade is that you cannot buy it if you are 49, and premiums for a healthy 52-year-old on a short European break will often look expensive against a mainstream insurer.

key_facts.label: Annual multi-trip
key_facts.value: 180 days a year total, 45 days maximum per trip (extendable to 60–90 for some regions)

key_facts.label: Cover tiers
key_facts.value: Single trip: Essential, Standard, Plus · Annual: Standard, Plus

key_facts.label: Pre-existing conditions
key_facts.value: Most covered after medical screening — diagnosed conditions only

sections.heading: The limits are in a different league
sections.html:
Set the Plus tier against a mainstream insurer's top tier and the gap is stark:

  • Cancellation: £20,000 against a typical £5,000
  • Baggage: £10,000 against a typical £2,500
  • Medical: £20 million against a typical £15 million

The cancellation figure is the one that earns its keep. A couple booking a three-week escorted tour or an ocean cruise can easily commit £12,000 or more in non-refundable payments. That sits comfortably inside Saga's limit and well outside most competitors'.

The £10,000 baggage limit is similarly aimed at a specific customer — someone travelling with camera equipment, jewellery or medical devices, where £2,500 does not cover the contents of the case.

sections.heading: No upper age limit, and why that is rarer than it sounds
sections.html:
Most mainstream travel insurers taper away as you age. Annual policies often close to new customers at 75 or 79, and single-trip premiums climb steeply from 80 onwards. Some decline outright past 85.

Saga has no upper age limit on any policy. An 88-year-old can buy the same Plus cover as a 52-year-old, subject to medical screening.

For anyone in their eighties who still travels, that is often the difference between insured and uninsured. It is worth knowing that the specialist market for very elderly travellers is thin, and prices there are frequently worse than Saga's.

sections.heading: Medical screening: what 'diagnosed only' actually excludes
sections.html:
Saga covers most pre-existing conditions after screening, but with a specific and important restriction: only diagnosed conditions are covered. Anything undiagnosed or still under investigation is excluded.

That distinction catches people out. If you are waiting on test results, or have symptoms your GP is still investigating, that condition is not covered — and neither, potentially, is anything that turns out to be connected to it. The policy will cover a diagnosed heart condition you have declared; it will not cover chest pain you are being investigated for.

The practical advice is to complete screening after your diagnosis rather than during investigation, and to re-screen if your health changes between buying the policy and travelling. Declaring more is always safer than declaring less.

sections.heading: Cruise cover included, and the 180-day allowance
sections.html:
Most insurers treat cruising as an add-on, charging extra for cabin confinement, missed port departures and itinerary changes. Saga includes it as standard, which reflects who the product is for.

Trip length is generous too: 180 days on a single trip, against Aviva's 120. The annual policy allows 180 days of travel a year with a 45-day per-trip maximum, extendable to 60 or 90 days for some regions.

That combination — long trips, cruise cover as standard, no age cap — is aimed squarely at retired travellers taking extended winter breaks, and it is a coherent product for exactly that person.

sections.heading: Who should not buy this
sections.html:
Anyone under 50 cannot, and that is a hard line.

Beyond that, a healthy 52-year-old taking a £600 long weekend in Spain is paying for limits they will never approach. Twenty thousand pounds of cancellation cover on a £600 trip is dead weight, and a mainstream insurer's mid tier will almost certainly cost less for equivalent practical protection.

The value appears when the trip is expensive, long, or when your age or medical history makes mainstream insurers expensive or unwilling. Below that threshold, you are paying for headroom you cannot use.

pros: £20m emergency medical and £20,000 cancellation on the Plus tier — far above mainstream limits
No upper age limit on any policy
Cruise cover included as standard rather than charged as an add-on
Single trips up to 180 days, and 180 days a year on annual cover
£10,000 baggage limit suits travellers carrying valuable equipment
Most pre-existing conditions covered after screening
cons: Expensive relative to mainstream insurers for short, cheap trips
Only diagnosed conditions are covered — anything under investigation is excluded
Annual policies cap individual trips at 45 days despite the 180-day annual allowance
High limits are wasted on travellers who will never approach them
verdict: The right choice for expensive trips, long trips, cruises, and anyone whose age or medical history makes mainstream insurers awkward. The £20,000 cancellation limit and absent age cap are genuinely difficult to match elsewhere, and cruise cover as standard removes a common add-on cost. It is the wrong choice for a healthy person in their early fifties taking a cheap short break, where you are paying for headroom you will never use. If you are waiting on a diagnosis, complete medical screening once you have it — conditions under investigation are not covered.

faqs.q: Can I buy Saga travel insurance if I am under 50?
faqs.a: No. Fifty is the minimum age and there are no exceptions. Every Saga product is built around over-50s travellers.

faqs.q: Is there an upper age limit?
faqs.a: No. Saga has no upper age limit on any of its travel policies, which is unusual — many mainstream insurers close annual policies to new customers at 75 or 79.
Yes, as standard rather than as a paid add-on. Most insurers charge extra for cruise cover.

Saga covers pre-existing conditions that have been formally diagnosed and declared at screening. Conditions that are undiagnosed or still under investigation are excluded, along with anything that turns out to be related to them.

faqs.q: How long can I travel for?
faqs.a: Up to 180 days on a single trip. Annual policies allow 180 days of travel a year with a maximum of 45 days per trip, extendable to 60 or 90 days for some regions.
